text: AI’s efficiency promise has a catch.
You.
Every new AI tool promises the same thing. Work smarter. Save time. Focus on what matters.
Here’s what actually happens.
You do complete tasks faster.
Then your manager notices.
The efficiency gains don’t free up your time. They raise the baseline.
This isn’t new. The Jevons paradox.
Coal-fired engines didn’t reduce coal consumption. Consumption exploded.
AI does this to your capacity.
You’re the coal.
2x faster at writing emails?
You don’t write half as many. You write twice as many.
Your output doubled. Your capacity didn’t.
What actually helps. You need boundaries. 1. Define “done” before you start. Set the scope up front. Stop when you hit it.
2. Track what you eliminate, not what you produce. Measure time saved, not tasks completed.
3. Push back on scope creep. When someone says “but with AI you can just...”, the answer is “yes, and I’ve already allocated that capacity elsewhere.”
4. Use efficiency gains for recovery, not more work. If AI saves you two hours, spend one of them not working.
Decouple your value from your velocity.
If your role is purely about speed and volume, AI will eventually do it better than you.
The people who thrive aren’t the ones doing more.
They’re the ones deciding what’s worth doing at all.
That’s the skill to invest in.
